analysis.one_liner: Froze new federal regulations for up to a year while Congress drafted a regulatory overhaul.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed the regulatory moratorium 100-0 on March 29, 1995, the House gutted it two months later and inserted its own bill, and the two chambers never agreed on a final version before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: S. 219 would have barred federal agencies from taking nearly any new regulatory action — including just proposing a rule or publishing a notice — from November 20, 1994 until the earlier of December 31, 1995 or the day Congress enacted cost-benefit and risk-analysis requirements for rulemaking. Any covered rule issued during that window would have been suspended, statutory deadlines pushed back, and endangered-species listings and habitat designations frozen potentially through the end of 1996. Narrow exceptions covered imminent health or safety threats, criminal-law enforcement, civil rights (but not quotas or preferences), and a hand-picked list of industry-favored actions like telecom spectrum auctions.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses facing new federal rules — manufacturers, energy and mining firms, timber and real-estate interests affected by the Endangered Species Act freeze — would have gone a year or more with no new regulations, and any rule issued after November 20, 1994 would have been suspended. Businesses with 100 or fewer employees would have gotten an additional six-month delay on top of that. Specific carve-outs let textile importers, telecommunications companies, and securities exchanges keep moving on rulemakings favorable to them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Regulated industries facing new federal rules

how_it_helps.text: Banned federal agencies from taking any new regulatory rulemaking action — including merely proposing a rule — from November 20, 1994 until the earlier of December 31, 1995 or the enactment of laws requiring cost-benefit and risk analysis for rulemaking.
Suspended the effectiveness of any covered rule issued during the moratorium window, pulling rules already off the shelf back off the books.
Froze endangered-species listings and critical-habitat designations under a separate, longer clock, potentially through December 31, 1996.
Gave businesses with 100 or fewer employees a further six-month delay on any affected rule, on top of the moratorium itself.

Exempted by name the rulemakings that benefited particular industries: textile-import and customs rules, China trade-sanctions actions, FCC spectrum transfers and license auctions, and SEC rules to increase competition among stock exchanges.
Extended any statutory, regulatory, or judicial deadline dependent on a frozen rulemaking by five months or until the moratorium ended, whichever came later.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people would have waited for new protections: any federal rule touching health, safety, the environment, or the workplace could have been frozen for a year or more, and rules already issued would have been suspended. The emergency waiver for imminent threats required written approval from one political appointee in the White House budget office, and the bill barred people from suing agencies over violations of the moratorium, so someone harmed by a frozen rule would have had no enforcement tool of their own.
analysis.who_pays_short: Anyone awaiting new federal health and safety rules

drawbacks.text: New protections for health, safety, and the environment would have been stalled for up to a year — longer for anything involving endangered species — while the underlying hazards kept operating under old rules.

Waivers for imminent health or safety threats required a written finding by the administrator of the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs, a single political appointee, and the final bill expressly barred private lawsuits against agencies for violating the freeze.

The good-faith case for it: supporters argued agencies were rushing out a wave of rules in the months after the November 1994 election, and that a pause — with a published inventory of what had been issued — would give Congress room to enact cost-benefit and standardized risk-analysis requirements. The bill did exempt aviation safety, banking soundness, monetary policy, and civil rights rulemaking.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stated purpose — a pause while Congress rewrote the rulemaking process — was a real policy debate, but the bill's design tilted one way: it stopped everything while allowing only a named list of industry-favored rulemakings to continue, and it removed enforcement power from anyone the freeze actually harmed. The costs fell on people waiting for new protections; the benefits fell on the businesses those protections would have covered. It never became law, so neither side collected.

outcome.mechanism: Both chambers passed different versions — the Senate 100-0, the House by gutting the bill and inserting its own text — but the conference to merge them never produced an agreement, and the bill died when the Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Introduced January 12, 1995 by Sen. Don Nickles with 37 Republican cosponsors; the Governmental Affairs Committee held hearings, marked it up, and reported it favorably with a substitute amendment.
The Senate passed it 100-0 on March 29, 1995 — all 54 Republicans and all 46 Democrats voting yes.
On May 17, 1995 the House agreed to strike everything after the enacting clause of the Senate bill and insert the text of its own bill, H.R. 450, then passed the result without objection.

On June 16, 1995 the Senate disagreed to the House amendment, requested a conference, and appointed seven conferees; the record shows no conference agreement and no House conferees, and the bill never became law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The public, in the narrow sense that the regulatory freeze never took effect and agencies kept issuing health, safety, and environmental rules. The trade the bill was built around — a moratorium in exchange for cost-benefit requirements — failed, so regulated industries got neither the freeze nor the new process.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public; the freeze never took effect

industries.industry: Manufacturers and energy, mining, and chemical firms
industries.note: A freeze on all new rulemaking, including proposed rules and even agency notices, plus suspension of rules issued after November 20, 1994, would have stopped new obligations before they could take effect. The cost is delayed health, safety, and environmental protections for everyone else.

industries.industry: Timber and real estate interests affected by the Endangered Species Act
industries.note: The bill froze endangered-species listings and critical-habitat designations until the earlier of December 31, 1996 or the enactment of an ESA appropriations law, delaying protections for species on land these industries use.
Any affected rule would have been pushed back an additional six months beyond the moratorium for these firms, delaying compliance obligations but also delaying whatever the rule was meant to fix.

The moratorium exempted FCC rulemakings to transfer spectrum to private use and run competitive license auctions, letting those proceed while everything else froze. Industry gained licenses and spectrum; the public also gained auction revenue and new services, so interests ran partly together.
SEC rulemaking to increase competition among stock exchanges was expressly exempted from the freeze, keeping that pro-competition action on track.

Rules on textile imports, customs modernization, and China trade actions were exempted so enforcement and implementation could continue; these served both domestic apparel producers and trade enforcement rather than delaying protections.
